newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine traders see higher soybean area.
newsitem.headline: Argentine traders see higher soybean area.

text.p: Argentine farmers should sow more soybeans this year, including a larger proportion of higher-yielding first crop beans, due to changed relative prices and weather foiling wheat hopes, traders said Tuesday.

"My impression is that the area sown with soybeans is going to be substantial this year, and at least as much as last year's area," said Ricardo Baccarin, of Panagricola SAFICI. "Many farmers weren't able to sow wheat. They'll plant either soy, maize or sunflower, in that order of preference.
Baccarin said he expected maize area to rise from last year, but sunflower area would slip slightly.
Farmers sowed 6.7 million hectares with 1996/97 soybeans, according to the government's Agriculture Secretariat. Production was hit by a fierce drought, and totaled just 11 million tonnes.
Maize production was 14.7 million tonnes from 4.0 million hectares, and sunflower seed output 5.1 million tonnes from 3.1 million hectares.
With many farmers unable or unwilling to plant wheat before second crop soybeans in northern crop areas this season, the proportion opting for first soybeans should rise.
Baccarin said that up to 50 percent of this year's beans could be first crop soybeans, up from the usual 40 percent.
"I think soybean production could comfortably hit 13.5 million tonnes," he said.

A trader in the key soybean area of Rosario told Reuters that he also expected more bean area this season. But he stressed the extent of the increase will depend on whether bad weather succeeds in furthing pushing up U.S. maize prices and tempting wavering Argentine farmers into that crop.
"Our ideas on soybeans are still not very clear. It depends a lot on what happens to the U.S. maize price over the next few weeks," he said.

He said farmers in the areas of northern Buenos Aires province, eastern Cordoba and the province of Santa Fe had sown only half as much wheat this year, and the extra area will probably go to first crop soybeans.
He added that some farmers were already trying to sow maize, but were having problems with lack of rain.
"If it doesn't rain soon, they will have to wait and sow soybeans or sorghum," he said.
He said soybean farmers were pinning much hope this year on new genetically modified seeds resistant to Roundup weedkiller, which cuts costs for other chemicals.
"The transgenic seeds gave good yields last year even with the drought, and they reduce costs," the trader said.
He said that rain which has fallen throughout much of Argentina's grain belt over the past few days has missed more northerly farming lands.
But Baccarin said that 20-30 millimeters had fallen over much of the wheat, leaving the crop in good condition.
